analysis.one_liner: Removes legal immunity from dominant social media platforms whose moderation is not consistent with the First Amendment.
analysis.headline: With zero cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in subcommittee until the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the liability shield (Section 230) that lets websites host other people's posts without being sued as the publisher. Under it, a dominant platform would lose that shield unless its content moderation rules are 'reasonably consistent with the First Amendment' — rules that normally apply to the government, not private companies. It would also let anyone whose posts are banned, down-ranked, or demonetized by a dominant platform sue for up to $500,000 per incident, plus punitive and triple damages, and would strip immunity for a year from platforms that let illegal, obscene, or adult-minor exploitative content reach minors.
analysis.who_benefits: Speakers whose content is banned, down-ranked, or demonetized by a dominant platform, who would gain a new right to sue for large fixed damages; and parents/users who want platforms held liable when harmful content reaches minors. Platforms that are not dominant, and platforms that win FTC certification, keep their existing protections.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a private lawsuit for content providers subjected to bans, blocks, down-ranking, or demonetization by a dominant platform, with the greater of actual damages or $500,000 per incident, punitive damages for reckless conduct, and triple damages for willful failures [S3].

Strips a dominant platform of immunity for third-party content unless its moderation policies are 'reasonably consistent with the First Amendment' as applied to state actors, whether or not the platform is one [S3].

Removes immunity for one year from any provider or user that facilitates illegal online content, exploitative adult-minor contact, or content harmful to minors that is readily accessible to minors because the platform failed to screen minors out using available technology [S3][S2].

Requires the FTC and Attorney General to set up a certification process letting companies with over $500 million in net revenue seek a finding that they are not dominant, or that their moderation rules meet the First Amendment standard [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant social media platforms and their shareholders bear litigation exposure and large damage awards; users may also pay indirectly if platforms respond by removing more lawful speech to avoid lawsuits, or moderating less on the 'harmful to minors' carve-outs, and all large online services face new compliance and certification costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big social platforms and their investors

drawbacks.text: The bill applies First Amendment rules — written for government actors — to private companies, and pairs that vague standard with $500,000 fixed damages per incident and treble damages, which would flood dominant platforms with lawsuits and invite strategic litigation [S3].

To avoid the 'indecent, obscene, or harmful to minors' carve-out, platforms might over-remove lawful adult content or, conversely, curtail moderation generally, since the bill directs these exceptions be 'broadly construed' and a single violation strips immunity for a full year [S3].

Smaller platforms face costs too: any service over $500 million in revenue must seek FTC/Attorney General certification to establish it is not dominant, a new regulatory hurdle that favors incumbent scale [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responds to a real grievance — large platforms can suppress lawful speech with no recourse — and the fixed-damages right of action would give speakers real leverage. But the design is heavy-handed: a First Amendment standard for private companies is legally untested, the $500,000-per-incident formula invites mass litigation, and the year-long immunity waiver for 'harmful to minors' conduct could push platforms toward crude over-blocking. The benefits to ordinary speakers are plausible but speculative; the litigation and moderation chilling effects are more predictable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, and never came up for a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steube introduced the bill on January 26, 2023 and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On February 3, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors in either chamber [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill died without any vote on its merits [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant social media platforms keep their existing Section 230 liability shield and freedom to moderate as they see fit; content creators who claim censorship got no new legal remedy; any Member who preferred no Section 230 change did not have to cast a vote.

for.name: Rep. W. Gregory Steube
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Communications and Technology Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor-bound vote

sides.party_line_note: Only one Member of either party — a Republican sponsor — supported the bill; no cosponsors joined, and the record shows no votes on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Dominant social media and video platforms
industries.note: The bill strips their liability shield unless moderation meets a First Amendment standard and exposes them to $500,000-per-incident suits. Supporters say this restrains platform censorship of lawful speech; platform defenders argue liability threats would push companies to over-remove speech or keep legal-but-harmful content up.

Anyone demonetized, down-ranked, or banned by a dominant platform could sue for fixed damages plus treble amounts. Critics note this right of action could also be weaponized by spam accounts and trolls against platforms' enforcement of basic rules.

Even non-dominant companies must go through an FTC/Attorney General certification process to establish their status, adding compliance costs and a new regulator relationship, while the one-year immunity waiver for harmful-to-minors failures applies to all providers, not just dominant ones.
